questions.q: Why wasn't a real-time, direct integration with Prairie View's system ever actually an available option?
options: A real-time integration was available but rejected only because it was more expensive
Prairie View's homegrown system has no webhook or event capability at all, only a read endpoint, so there's no event to integrate on in real time
Prairie View refused to allow any integration under any design
ServiceNow cannot call any external REST endpoint on a schedule
questions.explain: Lesson 16 established that the constraint rules out real-time integration outright -- it isn't a harder version of the chosen design, it was never buildable against that system.

questions.q: What is the strongest real defense of building one domain-aware flow instead of three near-identical flows?
options: Three flows would have been faster to build than one
A single flow cannot be customized per hospital system under any circumstances
ServiceNow does not allow more than one Flow Designer flow per table
Three maintained copies create real risk of drifting out of sync with each other, while one flow proves the routing logic holds for every domain every time
questions.explain: One flow is the version that actually proves the architecture holds -- a Lakeshore request has to land correctly every time, not most of the time across copies that can quietly diverge.

questions.q: What's the honest answer to "nobody got exactly what they originally asked for in the category model"?
options: Requirements gathering did fail, and the category model should be rebuilt from scratch
Only St. Catherine's requirements actually mattered in the end

Requirements gathering surfaced a genuine structural conflict honestly, and the two-layer model is a documented compromise that addresses each side's real concern, not a failure to gather requirements
The conflict was invented by the implementation team and never actually existed
questions.explain: A real structural conflict between three legitimate ways of working doesn't have a solution where everyone gets everything -- the compromise addressing each side's core concern is the correct outcome, not a shortfall.

questions.q: Why pilot at St. Catherine's, the most mature and capable site, rather than the smallest or lowest-risk one?
options: St. Catherine's was chosen at random with no particular reasoning
Lakeshore and Prairie View were technically incapable of piloting anything
St. Catherine's has the smallest number of employees of the three systems

Its structured process makes its staff most likely to catch and precisely describe a real defect, turning the pilot into a genuine quality gate that protects the more trust-sensitive Lakeshore and Prairie View from absorbing the first round of problems
questions.explain: Lesson 18's reasoning is the opposite of "picked the easy one" -- using the most capable group first protects the two systems that can least afford a rocky first impression.

questions.q: What makes a panel-defense answer like these actually substantive, rather than a rehearsed line a real panel can see through?
options: It avoids naming any constraint that might make the decision look difficult
It's built only from the tradeoffs the build actually worked through -- the real constraint, the real alternative, and the real cost accepted
It restates the original decision more confidently without adding any new reasoning
It agrees with whatever framing the panel's question implies
questions.explain: Course 13's panel-defense lesson and this one both depend on answers grounded in real tradeoffs actually worked through, not a confident-sounding restatement of the conclusion.
